channel.description: Archive records from the Democracy in Crisis (20s) era

item.title: Jay Rosen on the digital revolution that wasn't
item.description: In CJR's Kicker podcast (Journalism 2050 series), Emily Bell and Heather Chaplin interview Rosen about the digital revolution that didn't deliver on its promises. He reflects on his 2006 essay 'The People Formerly Known as the Audience' and how what was initially understood as a technology of liberation became a mechanism of control and surveillance. The Financial Times data shows social media has become 'less social' -- the people formerly known as the audience are once again the audience.

item.title: Public journalism redux: Post-academia, Jay Rosen returns to where he started
item.description: Dan Kennedy profiles Rosen's post-retirement career move as president of News Creator Corps, a new organization that works with content creators to adopt journalism tools without giving up their independence. Kennedy traces Rosen's career from public journalism and Assignment Zero through his media criticism, noting this new role represents a return to Rosen's original mission of involving the public more directly in journalism.

item.title: Q&A with Jay Rosen: How Trump nullifies reality
item.description: Mark Jacob interviews the recently-retired Rosen about his concept of 'verification in reverse' -- taking established facts and introducing doubt to power political movements. Rosen explains how authoritarian rulers can nullify reality itself rather than just lying to the press, and offers recommendations for journalists including developing 'reality rejection checks,' treating denialism as a beat, and being aggressive in democracy's defense.

item.title: 36 thoughts on the 2024 campaign
item.description: Brian Beutler's election-day assessment of the 2024 presidential campaign, published as a numbered list of reflections. References Jay Rosen's 'not the odds but the stakes' framework as a test for the national press corps. Discusses press coverage failures, the fascism discourse, and what a Harris win or Trump win would mean for democracy. Partially paywalled.

item.title: A media critic urged 'not the odds, but the stakes.' Did it work?
item.description: Margaret Sullivan interviews Jay Rosen on the eve of the 2024 election about whether his influential phrase 'not the odds, but the stakes' changed campaign coverage. Rosen says it may have reminded journalists of what they already know but didn't fundamentally change the dynamic of horse-race coverage, which remains 'too easy, too available.' Sullivan argues Rosen's influence was greater than he admits, noting that many outlets organized coverage under 'stakes' framing.

item.title: The nonstop, dangerous Trump 'liestream' is same as it ever was
item.description: Andrew Revkin revisits a 2020 Sustain What conversation with Jay Rosen about presidential propaganda and the press's unpreparedness for it. Rosen is quoted extensively warning about 'the biggest propaganda moment in modern U.S. history.' The piece links to the full 2020 video discussion and connects it to the 2024 Trump campaign's disinformation strategy. Also recommends Mark Jacob's Stop the Presses and reviews a book on Musk's destruction of Twitter.

item.title: The political economy of normalization
item.description: An analysis of how mainstream institutions (news outlets, think tanks, universities) rehabilitate enemies of democracy through the revolving door, using the Ronna Romney McDaniel/NBC News hiring as the central case. Argues that 'normal' has multiple meanings and that the solution is to 'abnormalize' MAGA rather than asking institutions not to normalize it. References Jay Rosen's analysis of what service McDaniel could provide NBC regarding Trump's threats.

item.title: Lessons on how to cover politics in 2024
item.description: A year-end compilation episode where On The Media revisits 2023 political coverage to extract lessons for the 2024 election year. The episode includes excerpts from multiple guests, with Rosen's contribution drawn from the CNN impossible dilemma segment. It covers the threat to democracy, media accountability, and how journalism must adapt for an election cycle featuring Trump as a candidate.

item.title: Journalists tackle political puzzle for 2024
item.description: Article discusses challenges journalists face when covering Donald Trump and potential second presidency. Jay Rosen is mentioned in context of 'stakes journalism' - questioning what is at stake in an election.

item.title: CNN's impossible dilemma
item.description: Following CNN CEO Chris Licht's firing, Rosen and Gladstone discuss the impossible dilemma CNN faces: the network's Trump town hall was a disaster that demonstrated the failure of conventional formats, yet the 'business as usual' approach Licht promised advertisers was itself the problem. Rosen argues that journalism still needs an emergency mode and that the firehose of falsehood continues to overwhelm traditional coverage methods.

item.title: Fallout from Trump town hall: Jay Rosen on the tightrope news outlets face
item.description: Rosen returns to The 11th Hour to analyze the fallout from CNN's Trump town hall, which was widely criticized for giving Trump an unchallenged platform. He discusses the structural dilemma news organizations face when covering Trump: traditional formats like town halls and debates are exploited by a figure who operates outside normal political norms, yet ignoring him is not an option either.

item.title: One-on-one with Jay Rosen: Trump, conservative media, and the Ohio derailment
item.description: Rosen appears on The 11th Hour with Stephanie Ruhle to analyze how Trump and conservative media exploited the East Palestine, Ohio train derailment to attack the Biden White House. The segment examines the media dynamics of disaster coverage and how partisan outlets frame events for political advantage.

item.title: Jay Rosen on the mess at CNN and the perils of "both sides" journalism
item.description: Thor Benson interviews Jay Rosen for Public Notice about CNN's purge of Trump critics under new management, the perils of 'both sides' journalism, and why the decades-long campaign to convince journalists of 'liberal bias' ranks among the most successful propaganda campaigns in post-war America. Rosen advocates for pro-democracy journalism and suggests reframing political coverage as a three-way fight: MAGA, the Republican Party, and Democrats.

item.title: Brutal, reassuring and unvarnished
item.description: Opinion piece discussing coverage of the January 6th hearings by various news networks. The author praises networks for treating Americans as adults and contrasts this with Fox News's decision not to air the hearings, referencing Jay Rosen's sarcastic description of this as 'the public's right not to know.'

item.title: What does constructive journalism construct?
item.description: A keynote speech by Jay Rosen at the Bonn Institute on constructive journalism. The original German-language listing title translates to 'Jay Rosen on the question of what constructive journalism constructs.' The page was unavailable (404) at the time of scraping; content could not be extracted.

item.title: Jay Rosen says news outlets should be 'pro-democracy'
item.description: A CNN article summarizing Rosen's appearance on Reliable Sources, where he argues news outlets should openly identify as pro-democracy. He contends that major news organizations should be pro-truth, pro-science, pro-evidence, and pro-voting, and that taking these positions does not compromise journalistic integrity but rather defends the conditions that make journalism possible.

item.title: Journalists also have an obligation to fix democracy
item.description: Jennifer Rubin argues that mainstream media has been complicit in the crisis of democracy through trivialized coverage, false equivalency, amplification of GOP spin, and habitual treatment of Republican conduct as within normal political boundaries. The article discusses the press's obligation to actively support democratic norms rather than passively reporting on their erosion.

item.title: How to cover the ongoing siege on democracy
item.description: Rosen and Gladstone discuss how to cover democracy under sustained attack. Rosen introduces the truth sandwich method for reporting on misinformation, advocates for dedicated democracy beats at news organizations, and praises WITF's 'never forget' policy of contextualizing every GOP election story with the party's anti-democratic actions. He argues the civic emergency did not end with Trump leaving office.

item.title: Jay Rosen looks at what happened to journalism norms during the Trump years
item.description: Eric Black reviews and extensively excerpts a Rosen PressThink post examining the collapse of journalism norms during the Trump years. Rosen argues that norms like objectivity, balance, and the church-state separation between news and opinion were already weakening before Trump, but his presidency exposed them as unable to handle a political figure who systematically exploited them. The article includes reader comments debating Rosen's analysis.

item.title: Lucid Interview: Jay Rosen
item.description: Ruth Ben-Ghiat interviews Rosen about the press's struggles during the Trump administration. Rosen explains how presidential conventions became invisible assumptions that Trump exploited, discusses the dangers of expecting the press to function as political opposition, and identifies his central concern: that one of two major parties is anti-democratic and the political press doesn't know what to do about it.

item.title: What the press have and should have learned from the Trump era
item.description: Two days after Biden's inauguration, Gladstone assembles journalists including Yamiche Alcindor, Jay Rosen, Karen Attiah, David Leonhardt, and Masha Gessen to reflect on Trump-era lessons. Rosen advocates for pro-democracy, pro-voting, pro-truth journalism -- arguing that the press must take a stand for democratic values rather than hiding behind false neutrality. He pushes for journalism that openly supports the conditions that make journalism possible.

item.title: To protect democracy, journalists need to learn to think like hackers and spies
item.description: Rosen develops his threat modeling proposal for newsrooms, consulting former Facebook CSO Joshua Geltzer and national security expert Alex Stamos. Explains how threat modeling works in practice: identifying adversaries, mapping attack surfaces, running red team exercises, and creating a Threat Urgency Index. Argues newsrooms need these tools because traditional campaign coverage cannot address threats to democracy itself.

item.title: Four radical ways the media can protect US democracy from Trump
item.description: Rosen proposes four concrete recommendations for how the media should shift to 'emergency mode' in covering Trump: (1) stop covering live speeches/rallies, (2) suspend normal relations with the White House, (3) add an amplification check to every presidential quote, and (4) shift focus from what Trump says to what his government does. Then escalates to 'active threat' measures: create threat modeling teams, a live Threat Urgency Index, pressure officials to go on record, and track solutions instead of the horse race.

item.title: Journalists should be in 'emergency' mode
item.description: Rosen argues that journalism needs to switch to an emergency setting for covering the Trump era. Recorded during the 2020 dueling town halls, the conversation covers the citizen's agenda model, the firehose of falsehood, the limits of the view from nowhere, and why normal political coverage routines are inadequate for an abnormal presidency. Rosen urges journalists to recognize the civic emergency and adapt accordingly.

item.title: Don't let Trump be the protagonist of the pandemic (and four other ways the media can improve how it covers the coronavirus)
item.description: Five proposals for improving pandemic coverage: (1) End duplication through newsroom consortiums publishing simultaneously, (2) Create an Urgency Index ranking what the public should be most worried about, (3) Treat confusion as a governing style rather than isolated incidents, (4) Dislodge Trump from the 'protagonist' role in the COVID story, and (5) Track your own coverage metrics. Includes the viral 'plan is to have no plan' passage. Originally from PressThink.

item.title: In the 2020 US election, journalists need an agenda: defending democracy
item.description: Rosen argues that journalists covering the 2020 election need their own agenda to avoid being swept up in Trump's. He distinguishes between the 'properly political' and the 'overly politicised' in journalism, then proposes four specific agendas: a citizens agenda (asking voters what matters), fighting authoritarianism, evidence-based political debate, and pro-participation coverage. Originally published on PressThink.

item.title: What newsrooms can learn from threat modeling at Facebook
item.description: Rosen interviews Alex Stamos, former Facebook CSO, about how newsrooms could adapt corporate threat modeling for election coverage. Stamos explains threat modeling, threat ideation, red teaming, and tabletop exercises in detail, then applies each to a journalism context. They discuss how the 2016 GRU hack-and-leak campaign manipulated the press, how to prepare for similar 2020 attacks, and why newsrooms need internal guidelines for handling manipulated information. Published on The Verge.

item.title: The plan is to have no plan
item.description: A repost of Rosen's viral PressThink passage about the Trump administration's COVID response strategy: deliberate confusion, blame-shifting, and 'flooding the zone with shit' as a governing method. Originally published on PressThink in May 2020, republished by Adbusters magazine (issue #151).
